plan.topic_summary: Confidential computing uses hardware-based trusted execution environments to protect data while it is in use, extending security beyond encryption at rest and in transit. For a 1–5 year view, the key question is whether cloud providers and regulated industries will adopt it at scale, and whether performance costs and side-channel vulnerabilities will limit its practical deployment.
key_questions: Which cloud providers have shipped confidential computing to production, and what workloads are being migrated first (0–12 months)?
What measurable performance overhead do production workloads experience inside TEEs compared to unencrypted baselines, and is it acceptable for latency-sensitive use cases (0–12 months)?
What side-channel and enclave-escape vulnerabilities have been publicly demonstrated, and what is the typical remediation or mitigation timeline (1–3 years)?
What is the status of cross-vendor attestation standards and interoperability, and when might a single attestation framework become the de facto standard (1–3 years)?

Will confidential computing become a mandatory control in regulated industries such as finance, healthcare, and government procurement, and which compliance frameworks explicitly reference it (3–5 years)?

How does the expanded attack surface of confidential computing (attestation channels, enclave management, hypervisor interaction) compare to traditional encryption-only approaches, and what new threat vectors emerge at scale (3–5 years)?

sources.title: Survey of research on confidential computing
sources.abstract: Abstract As the global data strategy deepens and data elements accelerate integrating and flowing more rapidly, the demand for data security and privacy protection has become increasingly prominent. Confidential computing emerges as a crucial security technology to solve security and privacy problem, and it is also a hot subject of in contemporary security technologies. Leveraging collaborative security in both hardware and software, it builds a trusted execution environment to ensure confidentiality and integrity protection for data in use. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of the development process of confidential computing, summarizing its current research status and issues, which focuses on the security requirements for data security and privacy protection. Furthermore, it deeply analyses the common technical features of confidential computing, and proposes a trusted confidential computing architecture based on collaborative hardware and software trust. Then, it elaborates on the research status and issues of confidential computing from four aspects: hardware security, architecture and key technologies, applications, and standards and evaluation. Finally, this paper provides a synthesis and outlook for the future development of confidential computing. In summary, confidential computing is currently in a rapidly developing stage and will play an important role in cyber security in the future.

sources.title: Confidential Computing across Edge-to-Cloud for Machine Learning: A Survey Study
sources.abstract: Confidential computing has gained prominence due to the escalating volume of data-driven applications (e.g., machine learning and big data) and the acute desire for secure processing of sensitive data, particularly, across distributed environments, such as edge-to-cloud continuum. Provided that the works accomplished in this emerging area are scattered across various research fields, this paper aims at surveying the fundamental concepts, and cutting-edge software and hardware solutions developed for confidential computing using trusted execution environments, homomorphic encryption, and secure enclaves. We underscore the significance of building trust in both hardware and software levels and delve into their applications particularly for machine learning (ML) applications. While substantial progress has been made, there are some barely-explored areas that need extra attention from the researchers and practitioners in the community to improve confidentiality aspects, develop more robust attestation mechanisms, and to address vulnerabilities of the existing trusted execution environments. Providing a comprehensive taxonomy of the confidential computing landscape, this survey enables researchers to advance this field to ultimately ensure the secure processing of users' sensitive data across a multitude of applications and computing tiers.

sources.title: Confidential Computing
sources.abstract: Abstract The goal of confidential computing is to encrypt data in the system’s main memory without sacrificing performance. It protects data in use by performing the computation in a hardware-based trusted execution environment or secure multi-party computation. There are two approaches to protect the data in memory: full system memory encryption and individual virtual machine memory encryption, isolated from the hypervisor. Confidential computing encompasses different use cases across many critical industries. Nevertheless, the maturity of technical solutions must still be deployed at scale.

sources.title: CoVE: Towards Confidential Computing on RISC-V Platforms
sources.abstract: Multi-tenant computing platforms are typically comprised of several software and hardware components including platform firmware, host operating system kernel, virtualization monitor, and the actual tenant payloads that run on them (typically in a virtual machine, container, or application). This model is well established in large scale commercial deployment, but the downside is that all platform components and operators are in the Trusted Computing Base (TCB) of the tenant. This aspect is ill-suited for privacy-oriented workloads that aim to minimize the TCB footprint. Confidential computing presents a good stepping-stone towards providing a quantifiable TCB for computing. Confidential computing [1] requires the use of a HW-attested Trusted Execution Environments for data-in-use protection. The RISC-V architecture presents a strong foundation for meeting the requirements for Confidential Computing and other security paradigms in a clean slate manner. This paper describes a reference architecture and discusses ISA, non-ISA and system-on-chip (SoC) requirements for confidential computing on RISC-V Platforms. It discusses proposed ISA and non-ISA Extension for Confidential Virtual Machine for RISC-V platforms, referred to as CoVE.

sources.title: Machine Learning with Confidential Computing: A Systematization of Knowledge
sources.abstract: Privacy and security challenges in Machine Learning (ML) have become increasingly severe, along with ML’s pervasive development and the recent demonstration of large attack surfaces. As a mature system-oriented approach, Confidential Computing has been utilized in both academia and industry to mitigate privacy and security issues in various ML scenarios. In this article, the conjunction between ML and Confidential Computing is investigated. We systematize the prior work on Confidential Computing-assisted ML techniques that provide (i ) confidentiality guarantees and (ii ) integrity assurances and discuss their advanced features and drawbacks. Key challenges are further identified, and we provide dedicated analyses of the limitations in existing Trusted Execution Environment (TEE) systems for ML use cases. Finally, prospective works are discussed, including grounded privacy definitions for closed-loop protection, partitioned executions of efficient ML, dedicated TEE-assisted designs for ML, TEE-aware ML, and ML full pipeline guarantees. By providing these potential solutions in our systematization of knowledge, we aim to build the bridge to help achieve a much stronger TEE-enabled ML for privacy guarantees without introducing computation and system costs.

sources.title: Privacy-Preserving Decentralized AI with Confidential Computing
sources.abstract: This paper addresses privacy protection in decentralized Artificial Intelligence (AI) using Confidential Computing (CC) within the Atoma Network, a decentralized AI platform designed for the Web3 domain. Decentralized AI distributes AI services among multiple entities without centralized oversight, fostering transparency and robustness. However, this structure introduces significant privacy challenges, as sensitive assets such as proprietary models and personal data may be exposed to untrusted participants. Cryptography-based privacy protection techniques such as zero-knowledge machine learning (zkML) suffers prohibitive computational overhead. To address the limitation, we propose leveraging Confidential Computing (CC). Confidential Computing leverages hardware-based Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) to provide isolation for processing sensitive data, ensuring that both model parameters and user data remain secure, even in decentralized, potentially untrusted environments. While TEEs face a few limitations, we believe they can bridge the privacy gap in decentralized AI. We explore how we can integrate TEEs into Atoma's decentralized framework.

sources.title: Towards a Formally Verified Security Monitor for VM-based Confidential Computing
sources.venue: HASP '23: Proceedings of the 12th International Workshop on Hardware and Architectural Support for Security and Privacy, October 2023
sources.abstract: Confidential computing is a key technology for isolating high-assurance applications from the large amounts of untrusted code typical in modern systems. Existing confidential computing systems cannot be certified for use in critical applications, like systems controlling critical infrastructure, hardware security modules, or aircraft, as they lack formal verification. This paper presents an approach to formally modeling and proving a security monitor. It introduces a canonical architecture for virtual machine (VM)-based confidential computing systems. It abstracts processor-specific components and identifies a minimal set of hardware primitives required by a trusted security monitor to enforce security guarantees. We demonstrate our methodology and proposed approach with an example from our Rust implementation of the security monitor for RISC-V.

sources.title: Introduction to confidential computing
Evaluating the Performance of the DeepSeek Model in Confidential Computing Environment
sources.abstract: The increasing adoption of Large Language Models (LLMs) in cloud environments raises critical security concerns, particularly regarding model confidentiality and data privacy. Confidential computing, enabled by Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs), offers a promising solution to mitigate these risks. However, existing TEE implementations, primarily CPU-based, struggle to efficiently support the resource-intensive nature of LLM inference and training. In this work, we present the first evaluation of the DeepSeek model within a TEE-enabled confidential computing environment, specifically utilizing Intel Trust Domain Extensions (TDX). Our study benchmarks DeepSeek's performance across CPU-only, CPU-GPU hybrid, and TEE-based implementations. For smaller parameter sets, such as DeepSeek-R1-1.5B, the TDX implementation outperforms the CPU version in executing computations within a secure environment. It highlights the potential for efficiently deploying LLM models on resource-constrained systems while ensuring security. The overall GPU-to-CPU performance ratio averages 12 across different model sizes, with smaller models exhibiting a lower ratio. Additionally, we provide foundational insights and guidance on optimizing CPU-GPU confidential computing solutions for scalable and secure AI deployments. Our findings contribute to the advancement of privacy-preserving AI, paving the way for efficient and secure LLM inference in confidential computing environments.

sources.title: Confidential computing models
AI-Driven Confidential Computing across Edge-to-Cloud Continuum
sources.abstract: With the meteoric growth of technology, individuals and organizations are widely adopting cloud services to mitigate the burdens of maintenance. Despite its scalability and ease of use, many users who own sensitive data refrain from fully utilizing cloud services due to confidentiality concerns. Maintaining data confidentiality for data at rest and in transit has been widely explored but data remains vulnerable in the cloud while it is in use. This vulnerability is further elevated once the scope of computing spans across the edge-to-cloud continuum. Accordingly, the goal of this dissertation is to enable data confidentiality by adopting confidential computing across the continuum. Towards this goal, one approach we explore is to separate the intelligence aspect of data processing from the pattern-matching aspect. We present our approach to make confidential data clustering on the cloud, and then develop confidential search service across edge-to-cloud for unstructured text data. Our proposed clustering solution named ClusPr, performs topic-based clustering for static and dynamic datasets that improves cluster coherency up to 30%-to-60% when compared with other encryption-based clustering techniques. Our trusted enterprise search service named SAED, provides context-aware and personalized semantic search over confidential data across the continuum. We realized that enabling confidential computing across edge-to-cloud requires major contribution from the edge tiers particularly to run multiple Deep Learning (DL) services concurrently. This raises memory contention on the edge tier. To resolve this, we develop Edge-MultiAI framework to manage Neural Network (NN) models of DL applications such that it can meet the latency constraints of the DL applications without compromising inference accuracy.

sources.title: Combining Confidential Computing and Unikernels for Lightweight Confidential Computing
sources.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
sources.abstract: While the integrity and confidentiality of data can be guaranteed by confidential virtual machines (CVMs), this is only part of the chain-of-trust when deploying sensitive workloads on untrusted infrastructure. Any vulnerability inside the CVM can potentially undermine its integrity, making verification and hardening of the (full) software stack essential parts of the security of the system. Unikernels—library operating systems that statically link to the application to produce a minimal bootable image—are effective approaches to reduce the Trusted Computing Base (TCB). We present SEV-Unikernel, the first general purpose unikernel compatible with AMD’s CVM, SEV-SNP. SEV-Unikernel is language agnostic and runs in a standard hypervisor without any external dependencies. Our proto­type fully supports the native SEV attestation mechanism, enabling the measurement and attestation of the entire soft­ware stack and the proactive detection of integrity faults. We demonstrate the practicality of SEV-Unikernel on a variety of microbenchmarks and real-world workloads. Our experimental results show that SEV-Unikernel achieves a significant TCB reduction with respect to confidential Linux virtual machines. We observe almost no overhead on com­pute intensive workloads, but implementation weaknesses in the network stack cause a 1.3x to 12x overhead for network-intensive benchmarks.

sources.title: Cache Side-channel Attacks and Defenses of the Sliding Window Algorithm in TEEs
sources.venue: Design, Automation, and Test in Europe
sources.abstract: Trusted execution environments (TEEs) such as SGX on x86 and TrustZone on ARM are announced to protect trusted programs against even a malicious operation system (OS), however, they are still vulnerable to cache side-channel attacks. In the new threat model of TEEs, kernel-privileged attackers are more capable, thus the effectiveness of previous defenses needs to be carefully reevaluated. Aimed at the sliding window algorithm of RSA, this work analyzes the latest defenses from the TEE attacker's point of view and pinpoints their attack surfaces and vulnerabilities. The mainstream cryptography libraries are scrutinized, within which we attack and evaluate the implementations of Libgcrypt and Mbed TLS on a real-world ARM processor with TrustZone. Our attack successfully recovers the key of RSA in the latest Mbed TLS design when it adopts a small window size, despite Mbed TLS taking a significant role in the ecosystem of ARM TrustZone. The possible countermeasures are finally presented together with the corresponding costs.

sources.title: Fully Oblivious Differential Privacy for Frequency Estimation in the Augmented Shuffle Model with Trusted Processors
sources.abstract: In the shuffle model of DP (Differential Privacy), a shuffler randomly permutes users' data to achieve high accuracy and privacy. Recent studies show that most existing shuffle protocols are vulnerable to collusion attacks by the data collector and users. They address this issue by introducing the augmented shuffle model that incorporates random sampling and dummy data addition into the shuffler. However, it remains open how to ensure the shuffler follows the protocol and does not collude with the data collector in this model. We address this trust issue by thoroughly exploring the augmented shuffle model with TEEs (Trusted Execution Environments). We first introduce a new privacy notion, FODP (Fully Oblivious DP), which strengthens DP to prevent various TEE side-channel attacks based on external/internal memory access patterns and control flows. We propose a general framework for FODP algorithms based on memory-size obfuscation and three concrete algorithms within it. We also improve the efficiency of our algorithms by using the count-min sketch and optimizing the number of hashes. We evaluate our algorithms on Intel SGX and demonstrate their effectiveness through comparisons with nine baselines.

sources.title: Interface-Based Side Channel in TEE-Assisted Networked Services
sources.abstract: With the accelerating adaption of Cloud and Edge computing, cloud-based networked deployment emerges to enable providers to deliver services in a cost-effective and elastic manner. However, security concern remains one of the major obstacles to its wider adaption. Trusted Execution Environment (TEE) has been advocated to protect cloud services in an isolated execution environment. In this paper, we present a new genre of side-channel attack called interface-based side-channel attack and demonstrate its effectiveness on the TEE-assisted networked service system. The root cause of this attack is the input-dependent interface invocation (e.g., interface information and invocation patterns) that can be observed by untrusted software to reveal the control flows inside the enclave. Our evaluation demonstrates that the attack can effectively re-identify encrypted web pages processed in the SGX enclave with an accuracy of 87.6% and a recall of 76.6%, and can reduce the search domain of the 1024 bits RSA private keys to$1.69 \times 10^{-6}$of the original search domain. As countermeasures, we propose, implement and evaluate a set of static analysis tools to mitigate the newly discovered threats. The key idea is to use inter-procedural dataflow analysis to identify potential leakage via the interface, and then mitigate them during compilation using techniques including branch obfuscation, loop obfuscation, and constant size wrapper.

sources.title: CipherSteal: Stealing Input Data from TEE-Shielded Neural Networks with Ciphertext Side Channels
sources.venue: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (S&P)
sources.abstract: Shielding neural networks (NNs) from untrusted hosts with Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) has been increasingly adopted. Nevertheless, this paper shows that the confidentiality of NNs and user data is compromised by the recently disclosed ciphertext side channels in TEEs, which leak memory write patterns of TEE-shielded NNs to malicious hosts. While recent works have used ciphertext side channels to recover cryptographic key bits, the technique does not apply to NN inputs which are more complex and only have partial information leaked. We propose an automated input recovery framework, CipherSteal, and for the first time demonstrate the severe threat of ciphertext side channels to NN inputs. CipherSteal novelly recasts the input recovery as a two-step approach — information transformation and reconstruction — and proposes optimizations to fully utilize partial input information leaked in ciphertext side channels. We evaluate CipherSteal on diverse NNs (e.g., Transformer) and image/video inputs, and successfully recover visually identical inputs under different levels of attacker's pre-knowledge towards the target NNs and their inputs. We comprehensively evaluate two popular NN frameworks, TensorFlow and PyTorch, and NN executables generated by two recent NN compilers, TVM and Glow, and study their different attack surfaces. Moreover, we further steal the target NN's functionality by training a surrogate NN with our recovered inputs, and also leverage the surrogate NN to generate “white-box” adversarial examples, effectively manipulating the target NN's predictions.

sources.title: HyperTheft: Thieving Model Weights from TEE-Shielded Neural Networks via Ciphertext Side Channels
sources.venue: ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security (CCS)
sources.abstract: Trusted execution environments (TEEs) are widely employed to protect deep neural networks (DNNs) from untrusted hosts (e.g., hypervisors). By shielding DNNs as fully black-box via encryption, TEEs mitigate model weight leakage and its follow-up white-box attacks. However, this paper uncovers that the confidentiality of TEE-shielded DNNs can be violated due to an emerging threat towards TEEs: ciphertext side channels of TEEs create weight-dependent observations during a DNN's execution. Despite the potential of inferring DNN weights from ciphertext side channels, existing techniques are inapplicable due to their over-strong requirements and the high precision required by DNN weights. A DNN can have millions of weight elements, and even a few incorrectly recovered weight elements may make the DNN non-functional.

sources.title: PwrLeak: Exploiting Power Reporting Interface for Side-Channel Attacks on AMD SEV
CipherGuard: Compiler-aided Mitigation against Ciphertext Side-channel Attacks
sources.abstract: Recently, the new ciphertext side channels resulting from the deterministic memory encryption in Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs), enable ciphertexts to manifest identifiable patterns when being sequentially written to the same memory address. Attackers with read access to encrypted memory in TEEs can potentially deduce plaintexts by analyzing these changing ciphertext patterns. In this paper, we design CipherGuard, a compiler-based mitigation tool to counteract ciphertext side channels with high efficiency and security guarantees. CipherGuard is based on the LLVM ecosystem, and encompasses multiple defense strategies, including software-assisted probabilistic encryption, secret-aware register allocation, and diversion-based obfuscation. The design of CipherGuard demonstrates that compiler techniques are highly effective for fine-grained control over mitigation code generation and assisted component management. Through a comprehensive evaluation, it demonstrates that CipherGuard can strengthen the security of various cryptographic implementations more efficiently than existing state-of-the-art defense, i.e., CipherFix. In its most efficient strategy, CipherGuard incurs an average performance overhead of only 1.41X, with a maximum of 1.95X.

sources.title: ReminISCence: Trusted Monitoring Against Privileged Preemption Side-Channel Attacks
QuanShield: Protecting against Side-Channels Attacks using Self-Destructing Enclaves
sources.abstract: Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) allow user processes to create enclaves that protect security-sensitive computation against access from the OS kernel and the hypervisor. Recent work has shown that TEEs are vulnerable to side-channel attacks that allow an adversary to learn secrets shielded in enclaves. The majority of such attacks trigger exceptions or interrupts to trace the control or data flow of enclave execution. We propose QuanShield, a system that protects enclaves from side-channel attacks that interrupt enclave execution. The main idea behind QuanShield is to strengthen resource isolation by creating an interrupt-free environment on a dedicated CPU core for running enclaves in which enclaves terminate when interrupts occur. QuanShield avoids interrupts by exploiting the tickless scheduling mode supported by recent OS kernels. QuanShield then uses the save area (SA) of the enclave, which is used by the hardware to support interrupt handling, as a second stack. Through an LLVM-based compiler pass, QuanShield modifies enclave instructions to store/load memory references, such as function frame base addresses, to/from the SA. When an interrupt occurs, the hardware overwrites the data in the SA with CPU state, thus ensuring that enclave execution fails. Our evaluation shows that QuanShield significantly raises the bar for interrupt-based attacks with practical overhead.

sources.title: Obelix: Mitigating Side-Channels Through Dynamic Obfuscation
sources.venue: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (S&P)
sources.abstract: Trusted execution environments (TEEs) offer hardware-assisted means to protect code and data. However, as shown in numerous results over the years, attackers can use side-channels to leak data access patterns and even single-step the code. While the vendors are slowly introducing hardware-based countermeasures for some attacks, others will stay unaddressed. This makes a software-level countermeasure desirable, but current available solutions only address very specific attack vectors or have a narrow leakage model.In this work, we take a holistic view at the vulnerabilities of TEEs and design a tool named Obelix, which is the first to protect both code and data against a wide range of TEE attacks, from cache attacks over single-stepping to ciphertext side-channels. We analyze the practically achievable precision of state-of-the-art single-stepping tools, and present an algorithm which uses that knowledge to divide a program into uniform code blocks, that are indistinguishable for a strong attacker. By storing these blocks and the program data in oblivious RAM, the attacker cannot follow execution, effectively protecting both secret code and data. We describe how we automate our approach to make it available for developers who are unfamiliar with side-channels. As an obfuscation tool, Obelix comes with a considerable performance overhead, but compensates this with strong security guarantees and easy applicability without requiring any expert knowledge.

sources.title: ChaosINTC: A Secure Interrupt Management Mechanism against Interrupt-based Attacks on TEE
sources.abstract: For Trusted Execution Environment (TEE), interrupt-based side-channel attacks are becoming significant threats. Malicious supervisors use interrupts to perform single-step side-channel attacks or to improve the accuracy of existing side-channel attacks. This paper proposes a secure interrupt handle mechanism dedicated to TEE, named ChaosINTC. (1) To prevent frequent interrupts, a dynamic interrupt response delay mechanism delays the interrupt delivery with a variable time. (2) To prevent maliciously modifying ISRs, an interrupt handler protecting mechanism performs isolation and integrity checking. We deployed ChaosINTC on an open-source RISC-V core and evaluated its performance via FPGA. Our design provides strong security with marginal hardware and performance costs.

sources.title: Breaking Isolation: Last-level Cache Side-Channel Attacks on AWS Nitro Enclaves
sources.venue: Workshop on System Software for Trusted Execution (SysTEX)
sources.abstract: Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) safeguard the confidentiality and integrity of application code and data by creating isolated, secure memory regions known as enclaves, even in the presence of privileged adversaries with root or physical access. While TEEs such as Intel SGX, Intel TDX, and AMD SEV-SNP have been shown to be vulnerable to side-channel attacks, AWS Nitro Enclaves adopt a different design that avoids shared cores and memory regions. According to the AWS Whitepaper, by utilizing exclusive CPU cores and enforcing memory isolation through the Nitro Hypervisor, Nitro Enclaves prevent shared cache usage with other instances. The design treats cache-based side-channel attacks as impractical and outside the expected threat model.

findings.claim: Side-channel leakage is reported across several major TEE families (Intel SGX, ARM TrustZone, AMD SEV, AWS Nitro), so the claim that TEEs protect data from privileged software looks weaker in practice than in marketing.
findings.label: ai_interpretation
findings.rationale: Each paper attacks a different TEE (SGX interface channel, TrustZone cache attack, SEV power-reporting attack by title only, Nitro cache attack by title). The pattern is consistent, but each is a single lab demonstration. PwrLeak has no abstract. Real-world exploitation and vendor patch status are not covered by these abstracts. The Nitro paper's abstract is truncated, so its results are not confirmed.

findings.claim: Ciphertext side channels extend the TEE attack surface to AI workloads. Peer-reviewed work at S&P 2025 and CCS 2024 reports recovery of user inputs and model weights from TEE-shielded neural networks, which undercuts the premise of confidential AI inference.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: Two independent papers from top venues target different assets (inputs versus weights). The abstracts are partly truncated, so success rates and attacker assumptions (e.g. pre-knowledge of the target NN) are not visible. Practicality against production deployments is unknown.
findings.supporting_excerpt: the confidentiality of NNs and user data is compromised by the recently disclosed ciphertext side channels in TEEs

findings.claim: Ciphertext side channels appear to stem from deterministic memory encryption in the TEE design. Fixing them in software therefore means adding workarounds such as probabilistic encryption, register allocation changes and obfuscation, rather than a clean patch.
findings.label: ai_interpretation
findings.rationale: CipherGuard (an arXiv preprint, not peer reviewed) names deterministic memory encryption as the root cause and builds software-assisted probabilistic encryption to compensate. The abstracts do not say which hardware or generations are affected, or whether newer silicon removes the issue. Hardware-level resolution is an evidence gap.
findings.supporting_excerpt: new ciphertext side channels resulting from the deterministic memory encryption in Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs)

findings.claim: Software mitigations for TEE side channels carry real performance costs and are described as leaving gaps. Vendors' hardware countermeasures are described as slow and partial.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: Obelix (S&P 2024) states that strong protection requires oblivious RAM and obfuscation with a 'considerable' overhead and that some attacks will stay unaddressed by vendor hardware. CipherGuard (preprint) reports 1.41X average and 1.95X maximum overhead in its most efficient mode. Both are the authors' own evaluations on selected workloads. Overhead on large production workloads is not shown.
findings.supporting_excerpt: As an obfuscation tool, Obelix comes with a considerable performance overhead

findings.claim: Defenses are fragmented and attack-specific, resembling a patch-per-attack cycle. Separate mitigations target interrupt-based, ciphertext, cache and interface channels. Some are validated only on research platforms (an FPGA RISC-V core) or with vague cost claims.
findings.label: ai_interpretation
findings.rationale: Obelix says existing solutions address 'very specific attack vectors or have a narrow leakage model'. ChaosINTC was evaluated on an open-source RISC-V core on FPGA, not a commercial TEE. QuanShield (preprint) claims 'practical overhead' without figures in the abstract, and it works by terminating enclaves on interrupt, which may affect availability. ReminISCence has metadata only, so it is not assessed. No head-to-head comparison across defenses appears in these papers.

findings.claim: Cryptographic library hardening is not enough against kernel-privileged TEE attackers. An RSA key was recovered from the latest Mbed TLS on a real ARM TrustZone processor, although only with a small window size.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: This is a single 2023 conference paper. The attack is conditioned on a small window size, so its reach to default or hardened configurations is limited. The paper also lists countermeasures and their costs, but the abstract gives no details.
findings.supporting_excerpt: Our attack successfully recovers the key of RSA in the latest Mbed TLS design when it adopts a small window size

findings.claim: Vendor design arguments can be contradicted by independent research. AWS Nitro Enclaves are documented as treating cache side channels as impractical because of exclusive cores and memory isolation, yet a 2026 workshop paper titled 'Breaking Isolation' targets last-level cache attacks on them.
findings.label: ai_interpretation
findings.rationale: The abstract is truncated before any results. The title implies a successful attack, but the success rate, required attacker position and mitigations cannot be confirmed from the text provided. This is one workshop paper, and its peer-review rigor is unclear. Treat it as a signal to check the full paper.

findings.claim: Building privacy systems on TEEs requires extra algorithm-level obliviousness, because trusting the hardware alone is insufficient. This adds design complexity and a performance cost that the TEE pitch often omits.
findings.label: ai_interpretation
findings.rationale: This arXiv preprint (not peer reviewed) defines a new privacy notion, FODP, specifically to defend against TEE side channels. Evaluation is on Intel SGX only, against nine baselines. The abstract gives no overhead figures and no evidence on other TEEs.
findings.supporting_excerpt: We first introduce a new privacy notion, FODP (Fully Oblivious DP), which strengthens DP to prevent various TEE side-channel attacks

hype_flags: 'Protects against even a malicious OS or hypervisor': the papers show privileged-attacker side channels on SGX, TrustZone, SEV and possibly Nitro
'TEE-shielded models are black-box': ciphertext side-channel papers claim recovery of inputs and weights
'Nitro Enclaves make cache attacks impractical': a 2026 paper challenges this (abstract truncated, so the result is unconfirmed)
'Strong security with marginal cost': the ChaosINTC claim rests on an FPGA RISC-V prototype, and Obelix and CipherGuard report notable overheads
Treating TEEs as a generic privacy solution for AI: the evidence here is attack-focused and says nothing about mitigated production deployments

finding.claim: S3 overstates what the cited abstracts say. The Edge-to-Cloud survey lists attestation and TEE vulnerabilities as three parallel areas needing work, and 'improve confidentiality aspects' is one of them. Nothing in that abstract ranks them as 'the main' weaknesses or says they arise 'rather than' from the confidentiality concept. The ML SoK abstract speaks of 'limitations in existing TEE systems for ML use cases' and does not mention attestation. 'Repeatedly' and 'main' are not supported by two abstracts that each say something different.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The excerpt shows confidentiality improvement is listed as an open area alongside attestation and TEE vulnerabilities. This contradicts the S3 framing that the concept itself is not the problem. The SoK abstract does not mention attestation, so the 'repeatedly flags attestation' claim has only one abstract behind it.
finding.supporting_excerpt: improve confidentiality aspects, develop more robust attestation mechanisms, and to address vulnerabilities of the existing trusted execution environments
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

finding.claim: The findings leave out the side-channel literature, which directly undercuts the picture of confidential computing as a maturing data-in-use protection. Peer-reviewed work reports recovery of NN inputs and model weights from TEE-shielded workloads via ciphertext side channels. A 2026 workshop paper targets AWS Nitro Enclaves, whose vendor design treats cache attacks as out of scope. The CipherGuard abstract ties ciphertext leakage to 'deterministic memory encryption in TEEs', which looks like a design-level property rather than an incidental implementation bug. This weakens S3's 'not the concept itself' framing, S4's confidentiality-guarantee framing for ML, and the maturity narrative in S2.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The excerpt is from a peer-reviewed S&P 2025 abstract. HyperTheft (CCS 2024) makes a parallel claim for model weights. Both are attack papers evaluated by their own authors, so exploitability in production deployments is not established from abstracts alone. They still show that the Science set presents a one-sided, optimistic view of the guarantees.
finding.supporting_excerpt: this paper shows that the confidentiality of NNs and user data is compromised by the recently disclosed ciphertext side channels in TEEs
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

finding.claim: S5 attributes a CPU-versus-GPU gap to TEEs. In the abstract, the 'GPU-to-CPU performance ratio averages 12' compares hardware platforms. It does not measure the cost of confidentiality (TDX versus non-TDX on the same CPU). 'CPU-based TEEs struggle' is the authors' framing of the motivation, not a result of the benchmark. The only TEE-specific result in the abstract is that TDX outperformed a CPU-only run for a small model. That is a single arXiv preprint with no peer review, so S5's headline number cannot be read as a TEE overhead figure.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The ratio compares CPU and GPU runs. S5 presents it as evidence about TEE limits, a causal link the abstract does not establish.
finding.supporting_excerpt: The overall GPU-to-CPU performance ratio averages 12 across different model sizes, with smaller models exhibiting a lower ratio.
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

finding.claim: S1 presents 'without sacrificing performance' as part of the core definition. It comes from a single book chapter and states an aspiration. Other retrieved papers report non-trivial costs: considerable overhead for side-channel obfuscation (Obelix), and 1.3x to 12x for network-intensive workloads under SEV-Unikernel. S1 also gives the definition as TEE or MPC, whereas the Edge-to-Cloud survey includes homomorphic encryption in its scope. The finding should not be rated 'high' as a consensus definition.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The performance-free goal is reported in S1 as a feature of the field, while other cited papers (and Science's own S5 and S10) report overheads. The scope differences between abstracts show the definition is not uniform.
finding.supporting_excerpt: As an obfuscation tool, Obelix comes with a considerable performance overhead

finding.claim: S11 overstates 'hardware support is broadening' toward open ISAs. The evidence is a proposal paper (CoVE: 'proposed ISA and non-ISA Extension') and a formal-verification approach demonstrated on a Rust security-monitor example. Neither abstract reports shipping silicon or deployed attested RISC-V confidential VMs. The other RISC-V TEE item in the evidence set (ChaosINTC) was evaluated only on an open-source core on FPGA. This is design-stage research, not market or hardware broadening.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The word 'proposed' marks CoVE as an unratified design. The formal-verification abstract describes a methodology and one implementation example, so S11 reads a research direction as a trend in hardware availability.
finding.supporting_excerpt: It discusses proposed ISA and non-ISA Extension for Confidential Virtual Machine for RISC-V platforms, referred to as CoVE.

limitations: Abstracts only. Two papers (PwrLeak, ReminISCence) have metadata only, with no abstract, so they support almost no claims.
The CipherSteal, HyperTheft and Nitro abstracts are truncated, so attack results, success rates and mitigations are incomplete.

Only 12 papers, almost all about side channels in CPU TEEs, so risk coverage is narrow. The set has nothing on GPU or accelerator confidential computing, attestation and supply-chain trust, firmware bugs, fault injection, physical or DRAM attacks, cost or adoption barriers, or competing approaches (homomorphic encryption, MPC).
The set is biased toward attack and defense papers because of the risk-oriented queries. It cannot show how often attacks work in production or whether vendors have patched them.
Several mitigation papers are arXiv preprints (CipherGuard, QuanShield), which are not peer reviewed. Overhead numbers are the authors' own and depend on the workloads they chose.
Publication dates range from 2023 to 2026, and some attacks may have since been mitigated. The abstracts do not say.
Only titles, metadata and abstracts were available. Several abstracts (including src_027347b657) are truncated, and some papers have no abstract, so I cannot check what the full texts say.
The risk evidence set is dominated by TEE side-channel papers. It may under-represent counter-evidence such as vendor mitigations, successful production deployments and standards work.
The attack papers (CipherSteal, HyperTheft, Obelix and others) are evaluated by their own authors. I did not independently assess how practical they are against current hardware or patched firmware.
I left S4, S6, S7, S8, S9, S10 and S12 unchallenged: they are low-stakes and are scoped or hedged consistently with their abstracts, or are already correctly hedged.

sources.title: REGULATORY-COMPLIANT WRAPPER FOR PREDICTION MARKET CONTRACTS IN INSTITUTIONAL FINANCIAL INFRASTRUCTURE [US20260350633A1]
sources.abstract: [0000]    The invention provides a hardware-attested compliance wrapper for regulated prediction-market contracts. Native event-contract specifications, position records, and KYC data are processed inside a trusted execution environment under sealed, versioned rule sets. The system produces a wrapped instrument definition documenting institution-consumable compliance treatment of the native contract, assigns capital-treatment and reporting attributes, generates regulatory-reporting records, and emits a compliance attestation record binding the input commitments, rule-set versions, decision-tree path, capital methodology, reporting-schema transformation, and wrapped output to a hardware measurement. The resulting record can be independently verified by an institutional counterparty, regulator, supervisor, or reporting endpoint without relying on representations of the prediction-market exchange operator. The compliance attestation record includes the applied jurisdictional decision-tree path and the reporting-schema transformation log, enabling a relying party to independently reproduce the classification and reporting outputs from the committed rule-set data.

sources.title: HARDWARE-ATTESTED FEDERATED STACK ORCHESTRATOR FOR PREDICTION MARKETS [US20260350703A1]
sources.abstract: [0000]    A hardware-attested orchestrator coordinates, at a single regulated prediction market venue, a federated stack of companion compliance systems within a trusted execution environment. The orchestrator ingests attested outputs from Oracle Resolution, trade-integrity (HATIS), confidence-scoring (VPCS), and regulatory-wrapper (RCW) companions, validates each against its hardware-vendor attestation service, and binds them into a composite attestation chain. A cross-layer consistency engine enforces a committed constraint rule set sealed to the hardware, including resolution-timestamp alignment, downweighting of participants flagged by the VPCS-computed insider-risk indicator derived from HATIS signals, equality of confidence-scoring inputs across capital mapping and reporting, and jurisdictional correspondence. The orchestrator emits a master attestation quote binding the chain, consistency result, and unified stack output, independently verifiable by a regulator or institutional counterparty against the orchestrator and each companion without reliance on the venue operator.

sources.title: CLOUD SERVICE SYSTEM AND CONFIDENTIAL COMPUTING METHOD IN CLOUD SERVICE SYSTEM [WO2026228485A1]
sources.abstract: The present application provides a cloud service system and a confidential computing method in the cloud service system. A trusted execution environment in the cloud service system comprises an enclave virtual machine, and also comprises at least one physical device; the at least one physical device can perform data transmission with a storage device by means of a target device; and keys are configured in the at least one physical device and the target device, so that the target device is a trusted device, and the data is encrypted between the target device and the storage device. The solution provided in the present application can ensure that data is securely transmitted, and at least one physical device in a trusted execution environment can directly perform data transmission with a storage device, thereby bypassing a CPU, such that in a cloud service scenario, the data transmission efficiency can be improved, thereby accelerating confidential computing.

sources.title: METHOD FOR DATA PROCESSING AND RELATED DEVICE [EP4835699A1]
sources.abstract: [0001]    A method for data processing and related device. The method includes: calling an encryption-decryption circuit running in a trusted execution environment for first data using a program circuit running in a rich execution environment, wherein the first data is either plaintext data to be written to a storage device or ciphertext data to be read from the storage device; and acquiring the first data, performing a security processing operation on the first data, and returning second data acquired by the security processing operation to the program circuit in response to call of the program circuit, using the encryption-decryption circuit, wherein the security processing operation is an encryption operation or a decryption operation. The technical solution of the present disclosure can improve data security.

sources.title: HARDWARE-ANCHORED POLICY-GOVERNED ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE CODE GOVERNANCE SYSTEM [US20260342590A1]
sources.abstract: [0000]    A hardware-anchored system generates software code by an artificial intelligence model executing within a trusted execution environment (TEE). A cryptographic attestation module binds, as a single signed structure, a hardware-rooted measurement of the TEE, a model identifier, and the inputs to the generated code. Validation agents independently evaluate the code; a consensus engine produces a decision; and a policy enforcement engine determines acceptance against machine-readable constraints. A tamper-resistant provenance ledger records the inputs, code, attestation evidence, validation outputs, decision, and acceptance, and may anchor digests to a public blockchain. A deployment orchestrator deploys conditional on acceptance. The code, attestation evidence, and decision exist unencrypted only within the TEE and are tamper-evidently bound to the measurement, so an operator cannot alter or suppress them without invalidating the attestation.

sources.title: ACCEPTANCE-CONTROL LAYER FOR VERIFIED AI-GENERATED CODE [US20260339818A1]
sources.abstract: Disclosed is an acceptance-control layer for AI-generated software code, implemented as a system, method, and non-transitory computer-readable medium. A hardware-enforced deployment gate prevents transmission of candidate code outside a trusted execution environment (TEE) until four conditions are simultaneously satisfied: (i) a formal verification engine produces a machine-checkable proof of one or more correctness properties of the candidate code; (ii) a quantum-resistant cryptographic module produces attestation evidence binding the candidate code, the AI agents, and the proof to the hardware-rooted TEE measurement using one or more post-quantum cryptographic algorithms; (iii) a hardware-rooted consensus engine satisfies a policy-defined threshold among a plurality of validators whose eligibility is bound to the hardware-rooted measurement; and (iv) the candidate code, the proof, the attestation evidence, and the consensus decision are recorded in a tamper-evident provenance ledger supporting independent third-party verification.

sources.title: GOLF TEE FOR USE ON VARIOUS SURFACES AND AS BALL MARKER [US20260335734A1]
sources.abstract: A golf tee configured for use as a ball support and a ball marker is disclosed. The golf tee includes a body having a substantially smooth upper surface and a central opening extending between the smooth upper surface and a surface opposite the smooth upper surface, wherein the central opening is sized to receive at least a portion of a golf ball therethrough, and a plurality of legs extending downwardly from the surface opposite the smooth upper surface, the plurality of legs being configured to engage a ground surface so as to retain the body in a substantially upright orientation.

sources.title: HARDWARE-ATTESTED REGULATORY-COMPLIANT WRAPPER FOR PREDICTION MARKET INSTRUMENTS [US20260340724A1]
sources.abstract: [0000]    A hardware-attested system transforms native prediction market contracts into institutionally consumable wrapped derivative instruments within a trusted execution environment. The system ingests native contract specifications, position records, and pseudonymized participant-identity records, applies know-your-customer, anti-money-laundering, sanctions, and eligibility screening against a committed rule set sealed to the hardware, and integrates attested trade-integrity and confidence-scoring inputs from companion systems without recomputing them. A jurisdictional mapping module assigns a regulatory designation and a capital treatment mapping module assigns capital attributes under the Standardized Approach for Counterparty Credit Risk using a committed supervisory factor table and alpha multiplier. The system emits a compliance attestation record binding the wrapped instrument definition and capital attributes to the hardware and to commitments over the inputs and methodology, independently verifiable by a regulator or institutional counterparty against a hardware-vendor attestation service without reliance on the exchange operator.

sources.title: HARDWARE-ATTESTED TRADE INTEGRITY SYSTEM FOR PREDICTION MARKET EXCHANGES [US20260340723A1]
sources.abstract: A hardware-attested system detects trade-integrity violations at a prediction market exchange within a trusted execution environment. The system ingests order-flow and account-metadata records over an encrypted channel terminating within the enclave, computes cryptographic account-linkage fingerprints, and identifies groupings of accounts whose pairwise linkage scores exceed a configured threshold. A surveillance module generates raw trade-integrity signals classifying trade patterns as wash-trading, coordinated-trading, or collusion indicators, and makes these signals and the linkage fingerprints available for a companion scoring engine to compute a calibrated insider-risk indicator; the system itself performs detection only. An attestation module produces a hardware-attestation quote binding the surveillance code measurement, commitments to the ingested records and surveillance parameters, and the raw signals, verifiable by a relying party against a hardware-vendor attestation service independently of the exchange operator.

sources.title: HARDWARE-ATTESTED VERIFIED PREDICTION CONFIDENCE SCORING SYSTEM [US20260340195A1]
sources.abstract: [0000]    A hardware-attested system computes a signal-weighted probability estimate and a calibrated insider-risk indicator for prediction market contracts within a trusted execution environment. The system ingests participant position and pseudonymized identity records and receives raw trade-integrity signals as attested input from a companion detection system, which the scoring system consumes but does not generate. A participant-profiling module maintains sealed historical accuracy profiles from decay-weighted Brier scores, a conviction-weighting module computes capital-weighted conviction, and an insider-risk module computes a calibrated insider-risk indicator at a configured z-score threshold from the received signals and anomalous-accuracy patterns. A scoring module aggregates these into a probability estimate that downweights flagged participants. An attestation module produces a hardware-attestation quote binding the estimate, the indicator, and commitments over inputs and parameters, independently verifiable by a relying party against a hardware-vendor attestation service without reliance on the exchange operator.

sources.title: A POST-POSITION COMPLIANCE AUDIT METHOD AND SYSTEM [NL4002845A]
sources.abstract: [0001]    A post-position compliance audit method and system are provided, comprising modules including input acquisition, profile privacy processing, product risk extraction, a regulatory rule database, and jurisdiction triggering. The system collects user profiles, product information, recommendation results, and explanation texts, performs field minimization, interval desensitization, and trusted execution environment computation on the user profiles, and generates desensitized features to ensure privacy protection; extracts structured product risk features from multi-source materials; constructs a regulatory rule knowledge base, converts natural language rules into machine-executable logic, and triggers corresponding jurisdiction verification according to scenarios. The system integrates large-scale models and privacy computing to automatically verify recommendation suitability, detect compliance risks, review explanation texts, and generate traceable audit records. The present invention solves the problems of separation between recommendation and compliance, lagging rule updates, lack of explanations, and insufficient privacy protection, and improves recommendation compliance, accuracy, and security.

sources.title: TrustScore OS Auditable Importance Scoring with ZKP and TEE Attestations [US20260332418A1]
sources.abstract: TrustScore OS is a compliance-anchored platform that computes verifiable Importance Prediction Scores (IPS) by fusing cyclical engagement vectors with time-decayed historical influence vectors. The system embeds cryptographic compliance proofs, including zero-knowledge proofs and Trusted Execution Environment attestations, and issues machine-readable provenance tokens anchored to a tamper-evident ledger. It exposes privacy-preserving regulator APIs and standardized interoperability schemas for behavioral, emotional, and biological state representations. The platform integrates sustainability metrics, fairness auditing, human-in-the-loop governance, and programmable settlement mechanisms to enable regulator-aligned marketplace orchestration without disclosing raw personal data.

sources.title: SYSTEMS AND METHODS FOR RESERVING GOLF TEE TIMES [US20260330339A1]
sources.abstract: A computer-implemented system and method are disclosed for coordinating golf-related reservations. The system includes at least one processor and a non-transitory computer-readable storage medium storing instructions that cause the system to maintain a database of golf courses having associated tee time availability and course attribute data. The system receives search requests from user devices, generates available tee times based on the search requests, and enables reservation of selected tee times that are associated with user accounts. In some embodiments, the system further enables reservation of lodging accommodations, registration for golf scrambles, organization of group golf outings, and processing of payments. Course attributes may include landscape features used to filter search results. The system may operate as a cloud-based platform accessible via web browsers and mobile applications.

sources.title: HARDWARE-ATTESTED PREDICTION CONFIDENCE SCORING ENGINE [US20260330067A1]
sources.abstract: [0000]    A scoring engine executes within a hardware trusted execution environment to extract calibrated probability estimates from positions on a prediction market exchange. Position and pseudonymized identity records are confined to the environment. The engine maintains sealed accuracy profiles from decay-weighted Brier scores, computes capital-weighted conviction scores and computes a scalar information-asymmetry risk indicator from a domain z-score and pre-resolution timing concentration. A signal-weighted probability is aggregated by weighting each participant by a product of accuracy, conviction and a complement of the risk indicator, then calibrated with a confidence interval. A hardware-attestation quote signed by a hardware-rooted attestation key binds the measurement register, input and methodology commitments and the estimate, rendering code, input, methodology and output integrity independently verifiable against a hardware-vendor attestation service without the exchange operator, a result unobtainable by software-only computation. Commitments append to a tamper-evident ledger published to a public channel.

sources.title: HARDWARE-ATTESTED MULTI-EXCHANGE CONSOLIDATED PREDICTION MARKET PLATFORM [US20260330551A1]
sources.abstract: [0000]    A hardware-attested platform consolidates regulated prediction market activity across two or more exchanges within a trusted execution environment. The platform ingests per-venue federated stack orchestrator master attestation quotes, validates each against its hardware-vendor attestation service, and binds them into a composite attestation chain. A cross-exchange linkage engine relates participants across venues, a probability fusion module computes fused estimates for cross-listed contracts, and a cross-exchange consistency engine enforces a committed constraint rule set sealed to the hardware, including cross-venue insider-risk propagation, Oracle resolution agreement, fused-input equality, and aggregate position limits. The platform emits a platform-level master attestation quote binding the chain, consistency result, linkage-graph commitment, fused-probability record, and consolidated output, independently verifiable by a regulator or institutional counterparty against the platform and each participating exchange without reliance on any exchange operator.

sources.title: HARDWARE-ATTESTED ADVERSARIAL PREDICTION MARKET SURVEILLANCE SYSTEM [US20260330550A1]
sources.abstract: [0000]    A hardware-attested system performs adversarial integrity surveillance of multi-exchange prediction markets within a Trusted Execution Environment. The system ingests consolidated cross-venue attestation records, validates them, and maintains a rolling behavioral state comprising a participant identity graph, a calibrated probability surface, a venue microstructure history, and a cross-venue coordination index. An ensemble of at least six behavioral classifiers detects wash trading, coordinated inauthentic activity, probability manipulation, liquidity spoofing, cross-venue Sybil attacks, and insider trading, with a multi-classifier correlation boost applied when three or more classifiers flag a common participant. High-confidence detections yield cryptographically sealed adversarial alert records bound to platform and surveillance-system attestation quotes, zero-knowledge regulatory reports with credential-gated selective disclosure, and signed circuit-breaker recommendations to an orchestration system retaining decisional authority. Outputs are independently verifiable by a regulator without reliance on the venue operator.

sources.title: PRIVACY-PRESERVING, WEARABLE NON-INVASIVE SLEEP MONITORING DEVICE, SYSTEMS AND PROCESSES [WO2026222470A1]
sources.organization: NEUROACOUSTICS INC, INST TECNOLOGICO DE BUENOS AIRES
sources.abstract: Wearable devices, systems, and processes for non-invasive sleep monitoring and closed-loop stimulation are provided. In some embodiments, a wearable band supports electrodes positioned to acquire bioelectric signals during sleep, including signals usable to detect slow-wave sleep and determine a phase of a slow oscillation. A controller processes the signals and triggers sensory stimulation, such as acoustic stimulation including pink-noise bursts and/or vibratotile stimulation, according to timing based on the detected phase. The wearable device may include multi-channel amplification and filtering to improve signal quality. In some embodiments, privacy-preserving mechanisms protect sensitive sleep data by encrypting data at rest and/or in transit using cryptographic keys stored in a hardware security module or secure element and by performing protected processing in a trusted execution environment. Encrypted data may be transmitted to a docking station or other external computing system for analysis.

sources.title: Systems and methods for privacy-preserving multi-agent financial crime detection with cross-jurisdictional compliance management [US12770185B1]
sources.organization: LOHIA ANANNYA, DAS ALAK, GHOSH REETESH
sources.abstract: [0000]    A computer-implemented system for detecting financial crimes while preserving data privacy includes a multi-agent orchestration framework that coordinates autonomous agents configured for ingestion, pattern recognition, investigation, and reporting of financial transaction data. The system applies tokenization, jurisdiction-aware workflow management, and differential privacy safeguards, with a privacy-aware permission model and execution within confidential computing enclaves. These agents collaborate under access constraints to detect suspicious behavior and generate regulatory reports without exposing sensitive information.

draft.summary: Research activity on confidential computing is rising quickly: 113 works in 2024, 193 in 2025 (+70.8%), and 270 by 10 Dec 2026 against 139 at the same point in 2025 (+94%), so momentum is building in the current year [S2]. The literature defines the field as hardware-based protection of data in use [S1], although Risk challenge C4 notes the 'no performance sacrifice' goal is an aspiration. Commercial evidence is thin. Only Intel shows a shipping hardware product line [M1, M6], and the discovered service and software companies are very small or pre-revenue [M2, M3, K1]. The main uncertainty is security. Peer-reviewed side-channel work reports recovery of inputs and model weights from TEE-shielded neural networks, and the leakage may stem from design-level properties, which weakens the maturity story [R2, R3, C2]. Patent counts are noisy (golf-tee matches), dominated by one individual applicant, and flat year to date, so they say little [P1, P5]. Related stock prices are volatile and mostly in sharp drawdowns, which adds timing risk [T11].
draft.plain_summary: Confidential computing uses special processor features to keep data protected even while a computer is working on it. Research interest is growing fast, and Intel sells chips that support it, but there is little proof yet of paying customers. The biggest threat is that researchers keep finding ways to leak secrets from these protected areas, which could undermine trust in the approach.

themes.name: Hardware-isolated confidential computing in data-centre CPUs

horizons.label: forecast
horizons.assessment: Intel's 10-K confirms shipping SGX and TDX support [M1]. Research volume is still accelerating [S2]. Customer or revenue evidence is absent, Microsoft's retrieved filings do not mention the topic [M4], and Intel's price is in a steep, highly volatile drawdown [T9, T10]. The evidence supports 'available and heavily researched', not 'widely adopted'.

horizons.label: forecast
horizons.assessment: Whether this becomes a trusted baseline depends on side-channel defences. Current mitigations are fragmented, attack-specific and costly [R4, R5], and ciphertext leakage may be design-level [R3, C2]. Formal verification and a smaller trusted computing base are being pursued [S6, S7], but surveys say maturity still needs large-scale deployment [S2]. Evidence for deployment at scale is not in the findings.

horizons.label: forecast
horizons.assessment: The findings say almost nothing directly about this horizon. RISC-V confidential-VM designs are proposals or FPGA-stage work [S11, C5], and hardware countermeasures are described as slow and partial [R4]. Any long-term outcome is speculative.

bull.label: forecast
bull.narrative: Research momentum continues [S2]. Hardware vendors ship TDX/SGX-class features [M1] and fix leakage at the hardware level. Formal verification [S7] and reduced trusted computing bases [S6] open regulated and critical uses. Patent filings show cloud and chip applicants optimising TEE data paths [P3].

base.label: forecast
base.narrative: Confidential computing stays a security option inside server and cloud products. Each side-channel attack is met with a targeted patch and a performance cost [R4, R5]. Adoption grows gradually, but the findings contain no adoption data to quantify it.

bear.label: forecast
bear.narrative: Side-channel research keeps showing that TEEs do not protect against privileged attackers in practice [R1, R6, R7]. Because the root cause may be deterministic memory encryption, software fixes stay workarounds [R3]. Buyers discount the guarantees, and mitigation overheads reduce the value proposition [R4, R8].
